title: Before the Basement Becomes a Bedroom: A Two-Person Radon Recheck
subtitle: A change in how you use your home is a useful moment to test for radon. Here’s how to plan the check, read the result and decide what to do next.
imageAlt: A couple in a basement room reviewing a radon test kit beside a notebook and an unfinished wall.

body: A new room deserves a new check

A basement can spend years as storage, a laundry area or a place people pass through briefly. Then a renovation changes its role: a desk goes in, a bedroom takes shape, or the family starts spending evenings downstairs. That shift is a practical reason to test for radon—not because a renovation necessarily creates the gas, but because people are about to use the space more often. The CDC recommends testing again when people begin using a lower level and after a major structural renovation. The EPA likewise identifies a change in which level household members occupy as a reason to consider retesting. [1] [2]

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can enter a building from the ground. It has no reliable smell or visible sign, so a tidy room, a recently finished wall or a neighbor’s test result cannot establish what is in your own home. EPA recommends testing the lowest level that could be used regularly; radon-related lung-cancer risk depends on the home's radon level and time spent there, among other factors. A change in use makes it sensible to get information about the specific space. [1] [3]
Test the space people will actually use

Before buying a kit, agree on the question you want it to answer: what is the radon level in the lower-level room where someone will sleep, work or spend regular time? Choose a test that is intended for the home and follow its instructions about placement. A kit’s directions matter: they specify where and how to set it up, how long it should remain in place, and how to return or read it. [1] Don’t substitute a convenient spot if the instructions specify a different location.

A test in another part of the house, or one taken before a major renovation, may not answer the question about the newly used space. [3] Nor does a neighbor’s reading settle it; homes can have different results even when they are close together. [3] The point is not to seek a particular number. It is to measure the home under the conditions the kit is designed for and keep enough information to understand what was measured.
Choose a test length that fits the decision

Short-term tests take from two to 90 days; long-term tests take more than 90 days. A short-term test can provide an initial reading sooner, while a longer test is more likely to reflect a year-round average because radon readings can vary over time. EPA’s guide notes that short-term results can fluctuate and explains the value of longer testing for understanding average conditions. [1] [3]

Timing depends on what you need to know. If you are deciding whether to move someone into a finished lower-level room, you may want an initial result before making that change. If you have flexibility and want a better picture of longer-term conditions, consider a long-term test. In either case, follow the kit’s requirements rather than improvising. A test is a measurement over a defined period, not a permanent guarantee: a later renovation or change in how the home is used can make a new check worthwhile.
Make the test a shared, simple project

Two people can divide the work without turning it into a technical contest. One person can read the instructions aloud and set up the kit; the other can write down the location, start date, expected end date and any handling instructions. Swap roles if that feels more natural. The useful thing is to keep the record clear enough that neither person has to rely on memory weeks later.

Before setting the test out, check the instructions together and agree on a spot that matches them. Keep the kit undisturbed for the specified duration. If the directions say to mail it to a laboratory, note the mailing deadline and follow the packaging steps; if the kit has another reading method, use the manufacturer’s process. Avoid treating an online description of a different kit as a replacement for the instructions in your own package. If something goes wrong—say the kit is moved, damaged or left out longer than directed—check with the provider about whether the measurement is still usable.

When the result arrives, write it down with the room, dates and test type. In the United States, EPA recommends fixing a home at 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) or higher. EPA recommends fixing a home at 4 pCi/L or higher, but a short-term result near 4 pCi/L is less certain as an estimate of the year-round average. If a reading reaches that level, consult your state radon office about qualified testers and next steps; EPA’s guide specifically points homeowners toward state radon offices for information about qualified professionals. [3]

A result below 4 pCi/L is not a promise that the level will never change. The reading describes the test conditions and period, so retain the record and consider retesting if the lower level begins regular use or a major structural renovation is completed. [1] [1] If the result is close to the action level, the kit’s guidance and your state or Tribal radon program can help you decide whether confirmation or professional advice makes sense. Don’t choose a mitigation system based only on a general online diagram: a qualified professional can assess the home and recommend an appropriate response.
Renovation is a prompt, not a verdict

It can be tempting to treat the test as a final inspection item, like checking a smoke alarm before moving furniture downstairs. It is better understood as one piece of home-health information. The result can help you make a decision now, and the record can help you make a later decision if the room’s use changes again. Keep the report with renovation documents or other household records, where both residents can find it.

If you rent, share ownership or have a contractor managing the work, clarify who will arrange testing and who will receive the result before the project is complete. Local rules and available services vary, so contact your state or Tribal radon program for local testing and mitigation resources. If the result calls for action, use qualified guidance rather than assuming that finishing, sealing or ventilating a room has resolved the issue. The test is a starting point for a decision, not a substitute for one.
Before furniture moves in, leave a record

At the next unhurried moment in the lower level, sit down together with the kit and its instructions before setting anything up. Choose the room that will see regular use, confirm the placement directions, and decide who will handle each step. In a shared note, record the room, test type, start date, expected finish date and where the result will be kept. If a major renovation is still underway, write down when you plan to retest after it is complete. Then let the person who will use the room most often check that the plan answers their question. A clear record—not a guessed result—is what you want to carry into the next decision.
